headline: Build AI Agents That Won't Delete Your Database with read-only defaults
summary: Learn how to safely build AI agents with guardrails to prevent data damage.
details: A single line in the system prompt saying 'you are a read-only assistant' can prevent an AI agent from deleting a database. However, this is not a reliable safety net. A better approach is to design agents with read-only access by default.
Start with a read-only system that can observe, analyze, and report but cannot write, delete, or execute. Promote the agent to write access only when proven necessary and controllable.

Use a proxy layer between the agent and external systems to validate requests against a policy. This policy defines what the agent can and cannot do, ensuring it never accesses production databases or APIs directly.
Require human-in-the-loop approval for write operations. Instead of a simple yes/no confirmation, ask the user to re-express the intent in their own words to prevent fatigue and errors.
Implement idempotency keys for mutation operations to prevent duplicate actions. Ensure every action is safe to call twice, and use a circuit breaker pattern to handle failures.
caption:
Can AI agents be trusted with your database? New strategies for safe deployment.

A single line in the system prompt saying 'you are a read-only assistant' can prevent an AI agent from deleting a database. However, this is not a reliable safety net. A better approach is to design agents with read-only access by default.

Start with a read-only system that can observe, analyze, and report but cannot write, delete, or execute. Promote the agent to write access only when proven necessary and controllable.

Use a proxy layer between the agent and external systems to validate requests against a policy. This policy defines what the agent can and cannot do, ensuring it never accesses production databases or APIs directly.

Require human-in-the-loop approval for write operations. Instead of a simple yes/no confirmation, ask the user to re-express the intent in their own words to prevent fatigue and errors.

Implement idempotency keys for mutation operations to prevent duplicate actions. Ensure every action is safe to call twice, and use a circuit breaker pattern to handle failures.

headline: Pinwheel launches retro landline phone for kids starting at $68
summary: A modern take on the classic household phone for children aged 5-10
details: Pinwheel Home is a new device designed to let children stay connected without smartphone distractions. It operates over Wi-Fi, eliminating the need for a phone jack.
The phone comes in two models: Spark ($68) and Classic ($79), with the latter featuring a retro-style handset and customizable stickers.
Parents control the device through Pinwheel's Caregiver Portal, approving contacts, blocking unknown callers, and setting calling schedules and time limits.
Future updates will introduce three-way calling and integration with Pinwheel's watches and smartphones.
The device is available now through Pinwheel's website and expected to launch on Amazon this fall.
